recall.define: Define archive, weak symbol, shared object, dynamic loader, global offset table and load address (LMA) without the glossary and name the source for each.
recall.distinguish: Give the distinction and an objdump or readelf observation for: section versus segment; VMA versus LMA; object file versus executable; symbol versus identifier; static library versus shared object.
recall.apply: A firmware image boots but global initialized data reads as zero. Using LMA, VMA, startup code and linker script, explain what the startup copy loop must do, which readelf -l fields reveal whether .data has distinct load and virtual addresses, and which term names the section the loop must clear separately.

entries.definition: A static library: an ar collection of object files with a symbol index from which the linker extracts only the members that resolve currently undefined symbols, in the order the archives appear on the command line; a member needed by a later object is not pulled in unless the archive is repeated or grouped.
idiom: put the archive after the objects that use it
entries.misconception: Linking an archive links all of it.

entries.definition: The rule that the linker resolves undefined symbols from inputs left to right, extracting archive members only for symbols undefined at the moment the archive is scanned; the reason an unresolved symbol can be fixed by reordering rather than by adding code.
entries.misconception: The order of linker inputs never matters.

entries.definition: A symbol with weak binding that a global definition of the same name overrides without a duplicate-definition error and that resolves to zero (or a null pointer) if nothing defines it; a toolchain feature with no ISO C counterpart, used for default handlers in vector tables.

authority.locator: Chapter 4 — Symbol Table, entry fields and Symbol Binding

entries.misconception: A weak definition in an archive member overrides a strong one (archive extraction rules decide first).

entries.definition: An ELF file built from position-independent code that the dynamic loader maps into a process at run time and binds through dynamic symbol resolution; it shares code pages across processes and defines an ABI boundary that must stay compatible across versions.

authority.locator: §7.10 Dynamic Linking with Shared Libraries, pp. 734–737

entries.misconception: A shared object is linked when the program is linked (it is resolved by the loader at run time).

entries.definition: The program interpreter (ld.so) named in a dynamically linked executable's PT_INTERP segment, which the kernel starts first; it maps the needed shared objects in search order, applies dynamic relocations and then jumps to the executable's entry point.

A per-object table of addresses filled by the loader so that position-independent code can reach global data and functions indirectly; the procedure linkage table pairs with it for lazy function binding.

authority.locator: §7.10 Dynamic Linking with Shared Libraries, pp. 734–737

entries.misconception: The GOT is a security feature (RELRO makes it read-only after binding; the table itself is a relocation mechanism).

entries.definition: The address at which a section's bytes are placed in the image (LMA), as opposed to the address at which the code expects to find them at run time (VMA); when they differ, as for .data in flash, startup code must copy the section from LMA to VMA before main.

The symbol the linker records as the program's entry point (ENTRY in a linker script, -e on the command line), which for a hosted program is _start and for Cortex-M firmware is irrelevant because the vector table, not the ELF header, selects the reset handler.
entries.misconception: Setting ENTRY changes where the microcontroller starts.

entries.definition: The linker's removal of unreferenced input sections (--gc-sections with per-function sections) to shrink an image; anything reached only through the vector table or by hardware must be protected with KEEP or it silently disappears.
entries.misconception: Garbage collection cannot remove code the program needs.

entries.definition: The linker's report of where every input section and symbol landed, which archive members were pulled in and why, and how much of each memory region is used; the first place to look for an unexpected size or a missing section.
entries.misconception: The map file is only for debugging link errors.

entries.definition: An input section that no SECTIONS rule of the linker script places, which the linker drops into an output section of its own choosing; in firmware it can land outside flash or at the wrong alignment, so scripts should either name every section or make orphans an error.

The ELF mechanism by which a shared object exports several versions of one symbol (memcpy@GLIBC_2.14) so that old programs keep the behavior they were linked against; the reason a binary built against a newer glibc may refuse to load on an older one.

authority.locator: §7.10 Dynamic Linking with Shared Libraries, pp. 734–737

entries.misconception: A shared library with the same soname is always compatible.

entries.definition: The PT_TLS program header describing the initialization image for thread-local storage, which the loader and libc copy for each thread and address through the thread pointer; the toolchain realization of the C thread storage duration.

authority.locator: §6.6 Thread-Local Storage — mechanism, __thread declarations and address lifetime

entries.misconception: Thread-local variables are stored in the stack.

entries.definition: Relocation read-only: a linker arrangement (-z relro, full with -z now) that places relocated data such as the global offset table in a segment the loader marks read-only after binding, removing it as an overwrite target.
entries.misconception: RELRO is on by default everywhere (distributions and toolchains differ).

entries.definition: Removing the symbol table, debug information and other non-loadable sections from an ELF file to shrink it; loadable segments are unaffected, so a stripped binary runs identically but backtraces and symbolic debugging need the separately kept debug file.

A link (-r) whose output is another relocatable object file combining the inputs without resolving external references or assigning final addresses; used to build incremental objects or to apply a linker script fragment before the final link.
entries.misconception: The linker always produces an executable.
